title: Ramp-to-Plateau: Cold Primer and Repeatability Playbook
content:
Purpose
This playbook documents a pragmatic, reproducible procedure for driving the serving runtime from cold/idle to steady throughput (plateau) and verifying repeatability across runs and machine variants. It focuses on: the cold primer (what to do when everything is cold), ramp patterns and stabilization heuristics, measures to make runs repeatable, and short troubleshooting guidance.

Intended audience
- Perf engineers running throughput experiments
- SREs validating capacity and autoscaling behavior
- Applied ML team members verifying model variant performance on dedicated pools

Problem statement / motivation
Benchmarks often disagree run-to-run due to differing priming states (KV cache, CUDA kernels loaded, JITed ops), bursty queues, and traffic arrival shapes. We need a concise, repeatable sequence that reliably (and quickly) takes a target model/server from cold to a measurable steady-state throughput while preserving the ability to compare across commits / hardware.

Key definitions
- Cold primer: a deterministic set of requests intended to populate caches and load kernels so subsequent throughput reflects steady-state serving, not transient startup effects.
- Ramp: controlled increase of offered load (qps / concurrency) until throughput saturates or target occupancy reached.
- Plateau (steady-state): a period where effective throughput and latency metrics are stable within a small tolerance.
- Occupancy: fraction of GPU/CPU capacity consumed by active inference work; tracked via device metrics + in-runtime request counters.

High-level approach
1) Pre-flight: validate test environment (node configs, Docker images, pin GPU clocks if applicable).
2) Cold primer: run a short, deterministic primer sequence to warm caches.
3) Ramp schedule: increase load with defined steps and hold times to surface steady-state behavior.
4) Plateau detection: apply statistical checks to decide when a hold period is stable enough to record measurements.
5) Repeat: perform N independent runs with identical seeds/configs and compare run-to-run variance.
6) Artifacts: store raw traces, device metrics, request logs, and loadgen configs with each run.

Detailed procedure
A. Pre-flight checklist (always run)
- Ensure model binary + tokenizer are the same commit/tag. Document model hash.
- Confirm runtime image tag and that all nodes were restarted at least once after image change.
- Pin CUDA/cuDNN versions on nodes; record driver version.
- Clear external caches (if using shared prefix caches) or isolate test pool.
- Start system monitoring (nvidia-smi / DCGM, node-exporter, runtime counters) and a high-resolution trace (1s or finer).

B. Cold primer (deterministic)
Goal: produce a consistent initial state for all runs.
- Primer should be small (30–120s) and deterministic: same tokens or short prompt set each run. Use 10–50 prompts that cover typical sequence lengths.
- Sequence: 3-stage primer recommended:
  1) Micro-warm (short prompt set at low qps, e.g., 2 qps) for 20s — wakes up HTTP stack and tiny kernels.
  2) Kernel-load stage (medium-length prompts, concurrency 4–8) for 30–60s — encourages JIT/FP kernel selection and loads larger attention kernels.
  3) KV/Prefix fill stage (longer prompts to populate KV cache) for 30–60s — ensure token-level caches are exercised.
- Record primer completion timestamps and a primer-id marker in traces so traces can be trimmed.
- Example primer loadgen CLI (custom loadgen):
  loadgen --targets 2 --duration 20 --prompts primer_short.txt --out=primer_micro.log
  loadgen --targets 6 --duration 45 --prompts primer_medium.txt --out=primer_kernel.log
  loadgen --targets 4 --duration 40 --prompts primer_long.txt --out=primer_kv.log
- Note: avoid over-priming; an excessively long primer can prefill non-representative cache states. We aim for consistency, not maximum cache fill.

C. Ramp schedule (example staircase)
- Choose a primary axis: offered QPS or concurrency. We usually use concurrency for GPU-bound workloads.
- Typical staircase steps (each step length = hold_duration):
  step 0: 10% target concurrency, hold 30s
  step 1: 30% target concurrency, hold 45s
  step 2: 50% target concurrency, hold 60s
  step 3: 70% target concurrency, hold 90s
  step 4: 90% target concurrency, hold 120s
  final: target concurrency (100%), hold 300s or until plateau confirmed
- During holds, collect per-second throughput and latency histograms.
- Rationale: long holds at upper steps are essential to let autoscaling/bursting and batching stabilise.

D. Plateau detection heuristic
- For each hold window (prefer the final target hold): compute the rolling 30s mean and standard deviation for TPS and P50/P95 latency.
- Accept plateau if over a 3x30s sliding windows the coefficient of variation (std/mean) < 0.03 for throughput and < 0.09 for p95 latency. These thresholds are conservative; tune per model.
- If plateau not reached in the scheduled time, extend the final hold by increments of 60s up to a max (e.g., +300s). If still not reached, mark run as "no-plateau" and capture detailed traces for root cause.

E. Repeatability and seeding
- Run N=5 independent experiments (cold-start each time including reboots of serving processes) and record: mean TPS, p50/p95, GPU util, kernel cache hits (if instrumented).
- Use the primer-id and exact loadgen config to ensure identical stimuli. Log random seeds and any RNG choices.
- Compare runs via: mean difference, standard deviation, and max-min spread. Flag if std(TPS)/mean(TPS) > 0.04 or if p95 variance exceeds 10% relative.

F. Data capture and artifacts
- Minimum artifacts per run (store in experiment archive):
  - loadgen config and prompt files (text)
  - request-level logs (JSONL) with timestamps and status codes
  - runtime traces (flame/trace log) and device metrics (nvidia-smi/DCGM) at 1s resolution
  - server logs and GC events
  - a small sample of responses (for quality regression checks)
  - summary CSV: second,tps,lat_p50,lat_p95,gpu_util

G. Post-run analysis checklist
- Trim primer windows from traces using primer-id markers.
- Recompute plateau windows and export a consolidated CSV for plotting.
- Produce: occupancy curve (offered load vs observed throughput), latency curve (p95 vs offered load), and drift plot across runs.
- Annotate any autoscaling events or fallbacks that occurred.

Common pitfalls and troubleshooting notes
- Apparent non-repeatability often caused by shared-system state (e.g., a central cache, other tenants). Ensure a dedicated test pool.
- Sudden throughput drops mid-hold: check for GC pauses, pod preemption, driver/kernel mismatches. Collect node dmesg.
- If warm runs beat cold runs significantly (>8% throughput delta), revisit primer: maybe primer is underfilling kernels. Try slightly longer kernel-load stage.
- If primer over-inflates performance (cold runs worse but hot runs unrealistically better), verify primer prompts are not biased toward easy-to-served sequences.

Quick reference: example commands
- Primer (single composite script):
  ./run_primer.sh --prompts primer_set/ --stages micro,mid,long --durations 20,45,40 --concurrency 2,6,4
- Ramp (example):
  ./loadgen --concurrency-sequence 8,24,40,56,72,80 --hold-secs 30,45,60,90,120,300 --prompts steady_prompts.txt --outdir runs/exp-20250109
- Collect metrics:
  ./collect_metrics.py --target-node pool-qa-03 --interval 1 --out runs/exp-20250109/metrics.csv

Open questions / TODOs
- Standardize a minimal cross-team primer prompt set that covers short/medium/long patterns while remaining unbiased.
- Explore automated plateau detection via change-point detection algorithms (off-the-shelf vs. simple CV threshold).
- Instrument kernel cache hit metrics from runtime for richer primer validation.

Appendix: suggested quick primer prompt set (example)
- short: 10 prompts avg 10 tokens (toy QA pairs)
- medium: 20 prompts avg 80 tokens (avg-sequence completion style)
- long: 10 prompts avg 250 tokens (few-shot context to exercise KV)

Notes and provenance
This doc was adapted from internal experiments run in 2024 on rdm-dedicated-pool with A100-80GB nodes. Results and thresholds are empirical starting points and must be revalidated per model family.

If you run experiments based on this playbook, attach the run archive link below and ping #perf to schedule a short sync to compare notes.
